name: Pushpavaneswarar Temple, Thiruppuvanam
deity: Shiva as Pushpavaneswarar (Poovananathar), with the goddess Soundaranayaki
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Pandya Nadu on the Vaigai, sung by Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar in the Tevaram (7th–8th century)
summary: On the bank of the Vaigai below Madurai, Shiva is worshipped as Pushpavaneswarar, Lord of the flower grove — the one Pandya Nadu shrine sung by all three Tevaram saints.

sections.history: Thiruppuvanam is a river town on the Vaigai, about 20 km south-east of Madurai on the road to Rameswaram. Its temple is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and holds a distinction among the fourteen of Pandya Nadu: it is remembered as the only one praised by all three Tevaram saints, Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar. Thiruppuvanam is also woven into Madurai's own sacred story, for one of the Thiruvilaiyadal, the divine sports of the Lord of Madurai, takes place here. Above all the town is known along the Vaigai as a place for ancestral rites, held by tradition to be as sanctifying as Kasi.
sections.architecture: A seven-tiered rajagopuram leads into the temple, with the sanctum of Pushpavaneswarar and a separate shrine for the goddess Soundaranayaki. The temple tank lies beside the complex, and the sthala purana names several sacred waters here — the Vaigai itself, the Manikarnikai, and theerthams of Vasishta and Indra. The Nandi before the sanctum is shown leaning slightly aside, a detail tied to Sambandar's visit. Across the river stands the Moovar Mandapam, which marks the spot where the three saints sang.
sections.legends: Tradition says Sambandar reached the far bank of the Vaigai and sang to the Lord without crossing, but Nandi stood in the way of his vision, and Shiva bade the bull to move aside. A second story, told in the Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam, is that of Ponnanaiyal, a devotee who longed to make a golden image of the Lord but had no gold; Shiva came to her as a wandering siddha and turned her metal vessels to gold overnight. The sthala purana adds that ashes of the dead brought here once turned into flowers.
sections.festivals: The Vaikasi Visakam brahmotsavam in May–June is the temple's great festival. The Aadi mulaikottu festival, Navaratri and the Aippasi kolattam are kept too, and on new-moon days, especially Aadi and Thai Amavasai, families gather on the Vaigai banks for ancestral rites; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Many come to Thiruppuvanam first for the river, performing tarpanam for their ancestors on the Vaigai's sandy banks before entering the temple. Inside, look for the leaning Nandi and pause before the Lord of the flower grove; then look across the river towards the Moovar Mandapam, where the saints are said to have stood and sung.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure; crowds are heavier on new-moon days. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors and at the riverbank rites, ask before taking pictures and respect families' privacy.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruppuvanam lies about 20 km south-east of Madurai on the Madurai–Rameswaram highway, with frequent buses from Madurai. The town has a small railway station on the Madurai–Manamadurai line; Madurai Junction and Madurai Airport are the nearest major hubs.
